nature-eecon-165.title: The environmental Kuznets curve: does growth clean up after itself?
nature-eecon-165.text:
Between 1970 and 2006, US real GDP grew 195%. Over the same years, sulfur dioxide emissions fell from 31 million tons to 15 million, and lead emissions fell by more than 98%. Numbers like these support the environmental Kuznets curve: the hypothesis that environmental damage worsens as an economy grows, until average income reaches a certain level, and then improves. It borrows the inverted-U shape of the {{ref:nature-eecon-164}}.

There is considerable evidence for the pattern in some indicators, especially water and air pollution from sulfur dioxide, lead and DDT. Net deforestation has ceased among countries with GDP per person of at least $4,600, though rich countries may be "exporting" their deforestation. The curve is a proposed model for {{ref:nature-eecon-147}}.

Other measures do not bend. Energy, land and resource use may not fall with rising income, and total energy use and many greenhouse gas emissions still rise in most developed countries. Carbon may not follow the curve because cutting CO2 brings little local benefit, unlike cutting lead: a tragedy of the commons. Some researchers find an "N" shape, with pollution rising again as income keeps growing, or argue pollution is simply moved to poorer countries. The curve holds for some local pollutants; for carbon, resources and biodiversity it is disputed.

nature-eecon-192.title: Resource intensity: how much nature each dollar costs
nature-eecon-192.text: Resource intensity is the amount of a resource, such as water, energy or materials, needed to produce, process and dispose of one unit of a good or service. Nationally it is the resource used per unit of GDP. High intensity means a high price or environmental cost for turning resources into GDP. It is the mirror image of {{ref:nature-eecon-193}}, which measures output per unit of resource; the goal is low intensity and high productivity. The OECD and UNEP use intensity indicators to track progress in {{ref:nature-eecon-147}}.

nature-eecon-188.title: Planned obsolescence: built to fail
nature-eecon-188.text: In the 1920s General Motors' Alfred P. Sloan Jr. faced a saturated car market. His answer was a new model every year, to keep sales up. Planned obsolescence is designing a product with an artificially short life or a deliberately weak design. After a set time, it stops working or looks out of date. The aim is to shorten the "replacement cycle" between purchases. It works best when a producer has at least an oligopoly, a market with few sellers. It also relies on buyers not knowing how long a product was designed to last. Competition pushes the other way: longer-lasting Japanese cars forced American carmakers to build more durable vehicles. In 2015 France set fines of up to €300,000 and up to two years in jail for planning product failure, the first legislature to recognize the practice. In the US, state right-to-repair laws target it. Philip Kotler sees competition and technology at work; Vance Packard called it wasteful and exploitative.

nature-eecon-198.title: World3: the model behind The Limits to Growth
nature-eecon-198.text: World3 is a {{ref:nature-es-077}} computer model simulating how population, industry, food production and Earth's ecosystem limits interact. Project manager {{ref:nature-hist-058}} and 16 researchers built it for {{ref:nature-eecon-154}} (1972), extending Jay Forrester's World2. It assumes non-renewable resources are finite and get harder to extract, so a growing share of industrial capital goes to extraction. In its reference run, world population peaked at seven billion in 2030. Persistent pollution peaked in 2035 at 11 times 1970s levels. {{ref:nature-hist-059}} trusted its qualitative conclusions, but some numerical parameters were "pure guesses". Vaclav Smil called lumping very different resources and pollutants into single variables meaningless. Yet a study in Yale's Journal of {{ref:nature-eecon-008}} found data broadly consistent with its projections. The model remains contested.

nature-eecon-173.title: Ecological overshoot: spending more than nature earns
nature-eecon-173.text: As of 2022, humanity used natural capital 71% faster than Earth renews it, Global Footprint Network estimated. That is ecological overshoot: demands on an ecosystem exceeding its ability to regenerate. Footprint accounts show humanity has been in global overshoot every year since 1970. William R. Catton Jr.'s 1980 book Overshoot is credited with the term's scientific use. Over 85% of the world's people live in countries in overshoot; a country whose footprint is smaller than its {{ref:nature-acct-047}} has an ecological reserve. Earth Overshoot Day marks the date each year when humanity's use exceeds what Earth can regenerate that year. Persistent overshoot points to continued deterioration and a possibly permanent fall in Earth's carrying capacity for people. WWF's Living Planet Report 2022 recorded a 69% decline in vertebrate populations since 1970.

nature-eecon-167.title: Agrowth: stop caring whether GDP grows
nature-eecon-167.text: Agrowth is the stance of being indifferent to GDP growth when designing policy. Its reasoning: GDP growth does not track real progress closely. In environmental policy it stands against both {{ref:nature-eecon-152}} and {{ref:nature-eecon-143}}. Economist Jeroen van den Bergh argues policy should neither chase nor avoid growth. It should use effective tools such as {{ref:nature-pol-084}}es or emission rights to price {{ref:nature-found-031}}s directly. Whether the economy then grows, stagnates or shrinks is of secondary importance.

nature-eecon-174.title: Ecomodernism: technology to make room for nature
nature-eecon-174.text: In April 2015, 18 self-described ecomodernists published An Ecomodernist Manifesto. Ecomodernism holds that technology can protect nature and improve human wellbeing by decoupling growth from environmental impact. It accepts replacing natural ecosystem services with energy, technology and synthetic solutions when that reduces impact. A key aim is to intensify human activity, through high-yield farming and dense cities, to leave more room for wild nature. It sets itself apart from ecological economics, degrowth, population reduction and the "soft energy" path. Eighteen ecological economists replied with "A Degrowth Response to an Ecomodernist Manifesto". Critics say it ignores mass extinction and the unequal sides of technological change, and degrowth and steady-state economists reject its confidence in decoupling.

nature-eecon-177.title: The Green New Deal: climate policy as jobs policy
nature-eecon-177.text: The Green New Deal borrows from Roosevelt's New Deal the idea that a crisis needs a huge public initiative. It calls for policy that tackles climate change while creating jobs, supporting growth and reducing inequality. On 22 October 2008, UNEP launched a Global Green New Deal in response to the Great Recession. In the UK, the Green New Deal Group and New Economics Foundation proposed one too. The 2019 US resolution by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ed Markey called for 100% renewable, zero-emission energy within 10 years. It also called for {{ref:nature-gov-168}} for communities of color, {{ref:nature-gov-184}} and low-income communities. The 2019 {{ref:nature-gov-135}} is less ambitious on timing, aiming for carbon neutrality in 2050. Many supporters doubt parts of it are feasible; one former US science adviser called the 2030 goal too optimistic.

nature-eecon-172.title: Eco-sufficiency: needing less in the first place
nature-eecon-172.text: A German study found sufficiency measures could theoretically cut household energy use by 70%. Eco-sufficiency shrinks a society's {{ref:nature-acct-027}} by moderating its demand for energy, carbon and material goods and services. As a goal, it means everyone living a good life within planetary boundaries; as a strategy, it means limiting consumption and production without threatening basic needs. The IPCC defines it as policies and daily practices that avoid demand for energy, materials, land and water while providing wellbeing for all. Thomas Princen popularized the term in his 2005 book The Logic of Sufficiency. Its proponents argue that efficiency's limits and {{ref:nature-eecon-159}} mean demand cannot fall enough without questioning the services themselves. Wolfgang Sachs's "Four D's" include decelerating, decentralizing and decommercializing. Critics fear it could hurt growth and raise unemployment, and its savings can trigger indirect rebounds.

nature-eecon-194.title: Sufficiency, efficiency, consistency: three roads to sustainability
nature-eecon-194.text:
Joseph Huber identified three classic ways to move toward {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, and each matches a camp in the growth debate.

Sufficiency cuts consumption and production without threatening human needs. It is the strategy of {{ref:nature-eecon-172}}, and it is linked to degrowth. Maria Sandberg distinguishes four kinds: absolute reduction, modal shifts such as changing how people travel, sharing, and longer product life.

Efficiency cuts resource use, energy or pollution per unit of output within existing systems. It is the strategy of {{ref:nature-eecon-191}}, and it has an affinity with green growth.

Consistency changes the system itself. It shifts to industrial metabolisms more in tune with nature's, such as renewable energy and circular design, and is rooted in {{ref:nature-eecon-008}}.

The three are not rivals so much as complements. Each answers a different question: how much we use, how well we use it, and what kind of flows we rely on.

nature-eecon-158.title: Post-growth: prosperity beyond GDP
nature-eecon-158.text: A 2023 study of nearly 800 climate policy researchers found 73% support post-growth: 45% agrowth and 28% degrowth. Post-growth is an umbrella term for views that accept endless growth cannot last on a finite planet. It moves the economy's main goal from GDP growth to well-being. Some scholars split it into {{ref:nature-eecon-143}} and {{ref:nature-eecon-167}}; others include doughnut, wellbeing and steady-state economics. Typical policies are shorter working time, universal basic income, wealth taxes, carbon taxes with strong redistribution, and universal basic services. Post-growth puts sustainability and social justice ahead of growth; degrowth goes further and calls for deliberately shrinking economic activity.

nature-eecon-178.title: The growth imperative: is the economy forced to grow?
nature-eecon-178.text: Can an economy stop growing without falling apart? The growth imperative says it may not be able to, because firms, households or governments face serious harm without growth. At the micro level, firms or households must raise revenue or consumption to protect their income. Marxist theory holds that competition forces firms to "grow or die"; critics reply that a firm can stay profitable without growth by paying profits out as dividends. At the macro level, a political imperative exists if growth is needed to avoid instability, which pushes goals such as climate action below growth. A central argument is unemployment: technical progress without growth destroys jobs (Okun's law). Proposed ways out include resource taxes, shorter working time and fairer income distribution such as basic income. Whether the concept is meaningful at all is disputed, even within {{ref:nature-eecon-158}}.

nature-eecon-160.title: Direct, indirect, economy-wide: three kinds of rebound
nature-eecon-160.text:
The economy can take back efficiency savings in three ways.

The direct rebound is the most obvious. A good becomes cheaper to use, so it is used more: cheaper driving leads to more driving.

The indirect rebound follows the money. Savings from an efficient cooling system are spent on something else, perhaps a luxury, which uses resources of its own. Indirect effects from household conservation can range from 10% to 200%, depending on the scenario.

The economy-wide rebound is the largest in scope. Cheaper services lower other prices, open new production possibilities and speed up economic growth.

The pieces add up in a way that surprises. Even if direct and indirect rebounds total less than 100%, the faster growth that efficiency brings can still raise the economy's total resource use. That is how the {{ref:nature-eecon-159}} can turn into the {{ref:nature-eecon-163}}.

nature-eecon-148.title: Relative and absolute decoupling: slower harm versus less harm
nature-eecon-148.text: {{ref:nature-hist-040}} noted that a dollar of GNP in 1969 used half the materials of a dollar in 1900. Yet total material consumption rose 400 percent. That is relative decoupling: impact per unit of output falls, but total impact can still rise. Absolute decoupling means total impact falls while output grows. For that, resource efficiency must rise at least as fast as output and keep improving. Between 1990 and 2015, carbon intensity per dollar of GDP fell 0.6% a year. But population and income per person each grew 1.3% a year, so emissions rose about 2% a year. Tim Jackson found much evidence of relative decoupling in the global economy, but evidence for absolute decoupling harder to find.

nature-eecon-151.title: Is decoupling happening fast enough?
nature-eecon-151.text:
Everyone in this debate agrees on the target: growth must be separated from environmental pressure fast enough to avoid serious damage. They disagree on whether that is happening, or can.

The skeptics have studies on their side. A 2020 study found no evidence of economy-wide decoupling nationally or internationally, and research has found absolute decoupling rare. Critics say nothing near the needed scale has been seen, so a sufficiency approach must complement efficiency. Hickel and Kallis model carbon intensity falling at most 4% a year. On that assumption, limiting warming to 1.5 °C is impossible, and 2 °C is reachable only if rich economies shrink by over 90%.

Rikard Warlenius replies that absolute decoupling faster than that 4% threshold has already happened, and that stronger policies could push it higher. He also argues that growth is better placed than degrowth to fund the deep, costly transitions the IPCC describes.

So degrowth scholars see no evidence of sufficient decoupling, while others point to fast cases and argue that policy, not physics, is the limit. The question builds directly on {{ref:nature-eecon-148}} and on the case for {{ref:nature-eecon-152}}.

nature-eecon-186.title: The rich and overconsumption
nature-eecon-186.text: The richest 1% emit more than double the carbon of the poorest 50% combined. A 2020 Oxfam-SEI report also found the top 10% of earners cause over half of global carbon emissions. The 2020 "Scientists' warning on affluence" linked growth-driven economies since World War II to rising inequality, resource use and environmental pressure. Proposed responses include progressive taxes on high-carbon activities, curbing luxury emissions and moving priorities from GDP growth to sustainability.

nature-eecon-141.title: Green economics: the economy as part of the ecosystem
nature-eecon-141.text: Green economics covers any economic theory that treats the economy as part of the ecosystem it sits within. It usually takes a holistic approach, mixing economic ideas with other subjects. Some economists treat it as a branch of established schools: {{ref:nature-hist-012}}, for example, with its old factor "land" widened into {{ref:nature-found-010}}. UNEP's growing commitment to natural capital and full cost accounting under the {{ref:nature-eecon-140}} banner could blur the lines between schools.

nature-eecon-142.title: Measuring how green an economy is
nature-eecon-142.text: Ordinary indices measure economic output and progress. Green economy indices arose to capture human ecological impact as well, along with efficiency and green investment. The Global Green Economy Index measures green economic performance, and perceptions of it, in 130 countries along four dimensions. Municipal governments also use ecological footprint measurements to gauge human impact.

nature-eecon-187.title: Overpopulation in ecology
nature-eecon-187.text: In ecology, overpopulation means a species' population is larger than the {{ref:nature-eco-593}} of its environment. It can follow higher birth rates, lower death rates, less predation or large migrations, leaving animals competing for food, space and resources. Judgments always mix facts and values: animals are often called overpopulated when they cause harm people care about. The concept is used mainly in wildlife management, for example for the worldwide rise in deer numbers. Predator–prey models are also used to set the maximum sustainable yield of fisheries.

nature-eecon-193.title: Resource productivity: more crop per drop
nature-eecon-193.text: "Crop per drop" sums up resource productivity: the amount of a good or service obtained for each unit of resource used, sometimes expressed as money earned per unit. Together with {{ref:nature-eecon-192}}, it is a key measure of attempts to decouple resource use from environmental damage. Research by Joachim Spangenberg suggests that a transition focused on resource productivity gives higher growth than business as usual while easing environmental pressure.

nature-eecon-144.title: What degrowth would actually do
nature-eecon-144.text: A 2022 survey of degrowth writing from 2005 to 2020 found 530 specific policy proposals. The ten most cited begin with universal basic income, shorter working time, job guarantees with a living wage and maximum income caps. Then come declining caps on resource use and emissions, not-for-profit cooperatives, deliberative forums, reclaiming the commons, ecovillages and housing cooperatives. Public support varies. In a Swedish survey, reduced working hours got about 50% support, a wealth tax 40%, a meat tax 30%, a maximum income 25% and a basic income 15%.

nature-eecon-182.title: Human population planning
nature-eecon-182.text: Nearly 40% of pregnancies worldwide are unintended, some 80 million a year. Population planning proposes to stabilize and then slowly reduce human numbers in response to {{ref:nature-eecon-180}}. Suggested approaches include better access to contraception and sex education, and lower infant mortality so parents need fewer children. Educating and empowering women and providing family planning have a demonstrated effect in lowering birthrates. Coercive measures, such as China's one-child policy and compulsory sterilization, have drawn strong criticism.
